plants.name: Camellia japonica
plants.description: An evergreen shrub with glossy dark green leaves and rose-like flowers. It thrives in mild, humid climates and is a cherished winter bloomer in gardens across the region.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to early spring (December to April in the Northern Hemisphere)
plants.location: Native to Japan, Korea, and China; widely cultivated in the southeastern United States, Western Europe, and the Pacific Northwest
plants.funFact: Camellia sinensis, a close relative, is the plant used to make all true tea, and Camellia japonica is the official state flower of Alabama.

plants.name: Prunus mume
plants.description: A small deciduous tree that produces fragrant blossoms on bare branches in the depths of winter. It is a powerful symbol of perseverance and hope in East Asian culture.
plants.bloomingSeason: Mid-winter to early spring (January to March)
plants.location: Native to southern China; cultivated in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, and in mild-winter gardens worldwide
plants.funFact: In Chinese culture, plum blossom is one of the 'Three Friends of Winter' along with pine and bamboo, and it blooms through snow.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: A striking shrub with the largest flower head of any protea, featuring a bowl of pointed pink bracts surrounding a central cluster of fuzzy florets. It is adapted to nutrient-poor, fire-prone fynbos habitats.
plants.bloomingSeason: Southern Hemisphere late spring to summer, with blooms from late spring through to autumn; peak around December to February in some regions
plants.location: Western and Southern Cape of South Africa; cultivated in Australia, California, and Hawaii
plants.funFact: The King Protea is South Africa's national flower, and the plant's genus is named after the Greek god Proteus, who could change his shape.

plants.name: Helleborus niger
plants.description: A low-growing perennial with cup-shaped white flowers that open in winter, sometimes pushing up through snow. The blooms age to a soft pinkish-green and last for weeks.
plants.location: Native to the mountains of central and southern Europe; popular in temperate gardens in Europe and North America
plants.funFact: Despite its common name, it is not a true rose, and all parts of the plant are toxic, which is why it was historically associated with folk medicine and witchcraft.
